Kolmogorov distance between a characteristic-function target and a mixture

Source: R/from_cf.R
gmm_cf_distance.Rd

For a direction \(a\), compares the distribution of \(a^\top X\) under the target with its distribution under the mixture and returns a lower and an upper bound for the largest absolute difference between the two distribution functions (the Kolmogorov distance). The differences are obtained by numerical inversion of the two characteristic functions (Gil-Pelaez, 1951), so neither distribution is sampled.

Usage

gmm_cf_distance(
  g,
  cf,
  direction = NULL,
  n_grid = 201L,
  probs = c(0.005, 0.995)
)

Arguments

g

A gmm or gmm_fit.

cf

The target's characteristic function, as in from_cf().

direction

Numeric vector with one entry for each dimension of g, not all zero. Default: the first coordinate axis.

n_grid

Number of grid points. Default 201L.

probs

The lowest and highest probability of the grid. Default c(0.005, 0.995).

Value

A list with distance (the largest difference on the grid), at (the grid point where it is attained), upper (the upper bound described above), upper_inside (the bound between the two quantiles in probs), truncation (a bound on the omitted part of the inversion integral from the highest frequency integrated to 20 times that frequency, added to upper and upper_inside; the part beyond is ignored), x (the grid), difference (target minus mixture distribution function at each grid point), and cutoff_gap (the modulus of the difference between the two characteristic functions at the highest frequency integrated). A cutoff_gap or truncation that is not small means the integral was cut off early, which happens when the target has a point mass or a very slowly decaying characteristic function. The bounds do not hold then.

Details

If upper is at most \(\varepsilon\), every quantile of the target's projection at probability \(q\) lies between the mixture's quantiles at probabilities \(q - \varepsilon\) and \(q + \varepsilon\).

distance is the largest difference at n_grid points, spaced equally in mixture probability between the two values in probs. It is a lower bound.

upper is an upper bound, valid when the characteristic function of the projected target is integrable and truncation and cutoff_gap are small. At a point between two grid points, the difference exceeds the larger end value by at most the probability step, and exceeds the nearer end value by at most half the spacing times a bound on the largest density difference. Outside the grid it adds the tail probability probs[1] or 1 - probs[2] to the difference at the nearest end. Move probs towards 0 and 1 to shrink the outside term.

References

Gil-Pelaez, J. (1951). Note on the inversion theorem. Biometrika, 38(3–4), 481–482. doi:10.1093/biomet/38.3-4.481

See also

from_cf(), gmm_cf().

Other diagnostics: bic_aic(), ess_summary(), ess_trace(), gmm_anneal_path(), gmm_conditional_entropy(), gmm_entropy(), gmm_evidence(), gmm_fit_ensemble(), gmm_fit_quality(), gmm_independence_graph(), gmm_mutual_information(), hellinger_mc(), kld_trace(), proxy_functional_ci()

Examples

## A normal target against a normal with a shifted mean.
cf <- function(t) exp(-0.5 * t[, 1]^2)
g <- gmm(weights = 1, means = list(0.1), covariances = list(matrix(1)))
gmm_cf_distance(g, cf)$distance
#> [1] 0.03987815
2 * pnorm(0.05) - 1
#> [1] 0.03987761
